procedural_history.originating_court: Original Jurisdiction: Supreme Court of India
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order No. 1953/59/Gl/G 3/T-19(11) dated 2nd February, 1981 issued by the Respondent State of Haryana to all Jail Superintendents in the State.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioners filed a Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 3226 of 1981 challenging the legality and/or validity of the Order dated 2nd February, 1981, arguing it violates Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution and illegally denies life convicts the benefit of set-off under sec. 428 Cr. P.C. They sought a mandamus directing the Respondent to consider them for premature release.

issue.issue_text: Whether the period of detention undergone by a convict as an undertrial prisoner can be set off against their sentence under Section 428 of the Criminal Procedure Code for the purpose of considering their case for premature release.

facts: The petitioners were life-convicts who argued that they were eligible for premature release.
Their eligibility depended on whether the time they spent in detention as undertrial prisoners could be counted towards their total sentence.

The Government of Haryana had issued an order stating that for life-convicts convicted before a certain date, the undertrial detention period would not be counted when considering them for premature release.
The petitioners challenged this order, claiming it illegally denied them the benefit of set-off provided under Section 428 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
law: Section 428 of the Cr.P.C. allows for the period of detention undergone by an accused as an undertrial to be set off against their sentence.
The crucial wording of Section 428 states that this benefit applies where an accused person has, on conviction, been "sentenced to imprisonment for a term."
application: The Court determined that the benefit of Section 428 is only available to convicts who have been sentenced to a specific, fixed term of imprisonment, not to those sentenced to life imprisonment.
The Court rejected the petitioners' first argument that a life sentence should be treated as a 'term' (e.g., 20 years) for the purpose of this section.
The Court also rejected the petitioners' second argument that the grant of remissions converts a life sentence into a 'sentence for a term', thereby making Section 428 applicable.
The Court reasoned that an order of remission is an executive act that only affects the execution of the sentence; it does not alter the original sentence of life imprisonment passed by the court.

Furthermore, the Court emphasized that Section 428 applies based on the sentence awarded by the court *at the time of conviction*. It does not become applicable later if the sentence is effectively shortened by executive actions like remission.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioners' claim, holding that the set-off for undertrial detention under Section 428 of the Cr.P.C. applies only to sentences of imprisonment for a fixed term and is not available to life convicts. The grant of remissions does not change the nature of the original sentence from life imprisonment to a term sentence, and therefore does not trigger the application of Section 428.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the period of detention undergone by a convict as an undertrial prisoner can be set off against their sentence under Section 428 of the Criminal Procedure Code for the purpose of considering their case for premature release.
appellant_arguments: A sentence of imprisonment for life should be considered as 'imprisonment for a term' because provisions in the Penal Code (Section 57) and Jail Manuals treat it as equivalent to a fixed term for calculation purposes.
Section 428 is a beneficent provision that should be interpreted broadly to be available to convicts sentenced to life imprisonment, as supported by a decision of the Gujarat High Court.
respondent_arguments: On a plain reading of Section 428, the provision only applies to persons sentenced to 'imprisonment for a term'.
A sentence of 'imprisonment for life' is not a sentence for a 'term', and therefore, the provision for setting off undertrial detention does not apply to life convicts.

cases.case_name: Rehman v. The State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: The view that Section 428 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not apply to convicts sentenced to life imprisonment is correct.

cases.case_name: Bhimsen v. The State of Rajasthan
cases.principle: The view that Section 428 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not apply to convicts sentenced to life imprisonment is correct.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Section 428 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not apply to individuals sentenced to imprisonment for life, as the section is exclusively for those who have been sentenced to imprisonment for a specific term.
obiter: Imprisonment for life means imprisonment for the remaining period of the convicted person's natural life, whereas imprisonment for a term means imprisonment for a definite or fixed period.
The view taken by the Supreme Court in Rehman v. The State of Maharashtra and by the Rajasthan High Court in Bhimsen v. The State of Rajasthan is correct.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: On a plain reading of Section 428 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the provision for setting off the period of undertrial detention applies only to an accused person who has been sentenced to 'imprisonment for a term'. Since the petitioners were sentenced to 'imprisonment for life', their cases do not fall within the section, and they are not entitled to this benefit for the purpose of considering premature release.
legal_tests_applied: Plain reading of the statutory text.
True construction of the statute to determine if a specific class (life-convicts) is comprised within its purview.
Consideration of the 'objects and reasons' of a legislative provision to understand the mischief it sought to remedy and the legislative intent.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the provision should be extended to life-convicts on equitable grounds, stating, 'The question is Dot wh~ther the beneficent provisiOn should bC ~xten-ded to life-conv_icts on a priori reasoning or equitable consideration but whether on. true construction the section comprises life-convicts within its purview and on construction it is not possible to hold that it does.'
The legislative intent, as derived from the 'objects and reasons' stated by the Joint Committee, made it clear that 'cases of life convicts were never intended. to be covered by th·e.provision.'
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the argument that a plain reading of the statute excludes life convicts, stating, 'On a plain reading of the aforesaid provision it will be clear that the cases of the petitioners, who have been sentenced to imprisonment for life, would not fall within the sectio11, for, the section applies to an accused person who bas on conviclion, been sentenced to imprison-on true construction the section comprises life convicts ~ithin its purview and on construction it is not possible to hold that they do.'
policy_considerations: The court considered the legislative intent behind the provision, noting that 'the mischief sought to be remedied has no rele-vance where gravity of offence requires the imposition' of imprisonment for life.
The court relied on the Joint Committee's report on the objects and reasons for introducing Section 428 to conclude that the provision was not intended to cover life convicts.
